body.text: The Digital Duty of Care Bill was already mired in a noisy controversy about freedom of expression. That debate will now be intensified by the horrific attack on independent MP Helen Haines.

Prime minister Anthony Albanese said this week that anonymity and the pace of social media have exacerbated rage and aggression, a phenomenon not confined to politics. “We are seeing a normalisation of the language of grievance and violence,” he said. “We must not conflate the robustness of Australian democracy with this rising tide of rage.”
I’ve spent the better part of the past decade researching Australia’s social media landscape, and I can tell you that too often these discussions are wildly off the mark.
Do social media companies amplify or deny free speech? Should they or shouldn’t they?

The discussion is stuck in a false binary, imagining that we can or should have only total free speech or absolute state repression. But the reality of Australia’s digital ecosystem is that, right now, neither of those options is even in play. Large foreign companies already decide the shape and structure of our public debate.

Every day, American social media platforms make business decisions that have thousands of big and small consequences for Australian discourse. These companies decide what Australians read online, what gets circulated, what gets buried, what gets promoted and who gets logged out of their accounts. We are living under Silicon Valley’s terms of service.

Research released last month showed, for example, how platforms’ decisions about which creators they pay, and what they pay them for, have fuelled a cottage industry of Sri Lankan creators churning out AI deepfakes of Australian politicians. This foreign-funded slop is now our news feed. And research released in the past week showed how even understanding what anorexia content is or isn’t blocked by the platforms depends on whether platforms will or won’t sue Australian researchers for doing the work. Their business decisions and interests already rule our digital airwaves.

Nobody in Australia voted for that. No Australian law designed it. It’s the by-product of commercial choices made elsewhere. While we’re all debating the possibilities for censorship, it’s worth remembering that this is hardly the free marketplace of ideas either.

So the real question is whether we want Australian rules, informed by Australian values, to decide how these platforms shape our public square, or whether we’re content to keep living under someone else’s terms of service. Right now we’re starting from a position of absolute influence and limited sovereignty.

Watch how the debate unfolds in the weeks to come. Ironically, what should be a debate about Australian sovereignty could become dominated by US-flavoured arguments about free speech. Expect American politics, American companies and American lobbyists to tell us their framing should be the most important one.

To be clear, debates about freedom always have merit and should always be discussed. But this is Australia. For us, living under Silicon Valley’s terms of service is not the same thing as freedom. It does us a disservice when we conflate the two.

One thing the bill offers should be uncontroversial: transparency. Right now, the Australian public and the people who make our laws can see remarkably little of what these platforms are doing to our discourse. We rely on company press releases, voluntary reports and whatever researchers can piece together from the outside.

The bill would change that. It would require transparency reports on harms and risk mitigation, and make platforms publish safety information. It proposes new protections for researchers studying online risks. It takes transparency beyond the limited corporate communications we get today.

None of this tells anyone what they can or can’t say. It tells us what’s already happening behind the scenes. If platforms are confident their systems serve Australians well, they should welcome the chance to show it. Europe already demands this kind of disclosure, and the exact same companies provide it there. There is no good reason Australians should get less.

In the end, this is about accountability. For too long, foreign companies have shaped our online world and harmed users, with little obligation to explain themselves or offer remedy to anyone here. This bill is a chance to put Australian rules in place and hold them to account. •
